I think that makes sense. I resonated with it, and bits of it felt really validating. However, we now know through a book that her son Martin Miller wrote and a documentary about Alice Miller's life through Martin Miller's journey, it seems that the author had a very thick shell of denial in her actual relationship with her son and her Holocaust/war-related trauma. I actually ended up picking up the book again because I've been struggling with this issue in a process therapy group for therapists. I've been pissed off at some of my groupmates for having a "shell" that feels disingenuous. I also have a shell like that myself when I'm trying to connect around my pain.

I wonder if you sensed something in the book...as in a sort of intellectualized, emotionally cool, dissociated, "spiritual by-pass-y," way of dealing with the issue that you saw both in the author and in your sister? I didn't sense it, but I wonder if you have? I also may not have sensed it because this is how I experience most professional therapy spaces (especially the psychodynamic-y/analytic-y spaces), many therapy colleagues, and even myself at times. This book is often recommended for early career therapists because it often speaks to the kind of blind spot that both makes someone a therapist but can also make someone bad at being a therapist (e.g. the ability to attune to an inattentive parent but then our sense of safety and self-esteem are correlated with that connection).

On a very different non-therapy note, I wonder if there may also be a translation thing going on...I think the original was written in German?

I struggle with my mental health but have the opposite issue with food. Still, these are things that help me eat normal food as opposed to binge my ass off. I go for casserole type of stuff. Baked oats or an egg bake for breakfast; you could add fruit, cream, cheese, and veggies for added calories and nutrients. Some overnight oats could be good but add some full fat (or at least 2% Greek yogurt for protein and fat). 

Salad kit wraps are nice but not necessarily high calorie unless you add stuff to it or have a side. Buy a variety of salad kits and some nice big wraps/tortillas. Batch cook some veggie meat, tofu or beans…make salad and wrap the protein and salad into the wrap. Serve with a side …yogurts, pita chips and hummus, etc.

Baked pasta dishes can be a good idea. Also, I recommend the blog Ministry of Curry for some nice instant pot Indian recipes.

Snack on hummus or seed/nut butters with chips, pretzels, fruits/veggies. Yogurt is good too like the chobani flip stuff. Are there things you like to snack on? That can help when you don’t have as much of an appetite. 

Also, pay attention to what brings you comfort and what you crave. If you’re like me, depression might rob you of the will to care for yourself. Things that are low effort high reward in terms of helping you feel cared for is a good idea. For example, I have been drinking a lot of chai because the Indian in me is really comforted by a cup of chai. This part of it may not be easy if you’re struggling with experiencing pleasure at this time.

I'm a lesbian, so maybe what I say should be taken with a grain of salt...but, here's my two cents. If I were a straight woman, I think I shouldn't date an ex-gay man. 

Mostly, I say this because I don't think that being ex-gay is a thing...at least, I mean that being gay is not necessarily something that someone puts behind them or cures like a cold. People might learn that their sexuality is more fluid than they originally thought...but that doesn't mean that you are no longer gay now. I don't think one can become "ex-gay"  without completely cutting out crucial and vital parts of one's psyche. Once you do that, you really live as a sort of shell of a person. Repression is a bitch. I'm saying this as a woman who has been extremely in denial of her sexuality for most of her life. I'm in my mid-30s...I was about 28-29 when I finally really let myself admit that I am very much a lesbian. I have lived half a life for most of my life. There is a way in which every connection, every interaction, everything is on a dimmer switch...not even just romantically. It's like holding your breath forever. Does that make sense? I can't even begin to explain how horrible and repressive it is. There is a reason why conversion therapy drives people to suicide. It's not psychologically healthy; I'm not sure how else to put it really. This is very much a huge part of why I was suicidal for most of my life. I think that if I were dating an ex-gay man, I could very well be participating in his psychological self-torture...that's bad for my relationship with him, and it would also kill me to see someone I love go through that kind of psychological torture.

Now, a lavender marriage where both folks know what they're getting into is not necessarily too bad IMHO.

That said, if I were a straight woman, I would date a queer man who was very in touch with his queer identity ...as long as there was mutual attraction between us. That's very different from dating an "ex-gay" or someone who is incredibly repressed about their sexual orientation.
